newsitem.title: UK: Blair determined to reform House of Lords.
newsitem.headline: Blair determined to reform House of Lords.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair on Wednesday signalled his determination to reform the House of Lords to prevent it frustrating his new Labour government.
Last week the government was defeated by 101 votes to 94 in the House of Lords on part of its plans to hold referendums on devolving power to Scotland and Wales by setting up assemblies.
The defeat was not fatal to the government's devolution plans, but it angered the new Labour government which was swept to a House of Commons majority of 179 in the May 1 election.

"What could be more wrong than the Conservative party depending on hereditary peers to do their business that they can't get through because they lost the election," Blair told the House of Commons during question time on Wednesday.
Labour promised in its manifesto to strip hereditary peers of the right to vote as the first stage in a reform to make the upper House more democratic and representative.
But Blair, juggling his priorities after the election, dropped the measure from his first legislative programme.

Aides to Blair said on Wednesday that there were no plans to bring the reform forward. But they said Blair's comments signalled a firm and growing determination to push the reform through when the government has time, probably next year.
Blair's statement "was the confirmation of a commitment which becomes firmer with every abuse from the House of Lords," a senior prime ministerial aide said.
The House of Lords is made up of peers who inherit their title and those appointed for prominent political or public service, along with some Anglican bishops and senior judges.
Only a small number of "working peers" take part in most business. But Labour argues that despite its landslide election triumph, the Conservatives have far more working peers.
The Conservatives can also call on so-called "backwoodsmen" -- who come to parliament only infrequently -- to back them up in crucial votes, leaving Labour at a huge disadvantage.
Peers are supposed to abide by a convention which states that they will not throw out measures contained in the manifesto of the party which wins an election.

But Labour believes last week's vote and other information gathered informally by Labour peers suggest the Conservatives, now reduced to just 164 of the 659 seats in the House of Commons, are prepared to break this unwritten convention.
Conservative peers dismiss the charge, saying they will only vote against manifesto commitments when the Labour government tries to curtail debate on issues of constitutional importance.
Peers in general can only delay and not scupper legislation. But a years delay at the start of Labour's first period of office in 18 years is significant, hence the government's anger.
Aides to Blair also suggested on Wednesday the government is considering naming a large number of new peers at the end of this month to redress the balance in "working peers".
Such a move would infuriate Conservatives. But there is little the opposition can do to stop Blair taking such action.
